title: Signed Rectified Flow: Negativity Controlled Generation
claim: Adding a negative target lets one generative model steer samples away from unwanted modes, concepts or training data.
layout: 8 panels: top row 2D toys, bottom row images, pink/blue borders
description: The figure is a gallery of eight panels, (a) to (h), that shows one idea across many uses. The top row has three 2D toy scatter plots. Each shows blue sample clouds before and after an arrow. Pink glowing crosses mark the negative regions that samples avoid. In (a) a red mode is suppressed. In (b) only the blue mode is kept. In (c) samples move away from individual data points. The bottom row has paired real images. Pink-bordered images are the baseline and blue-bordered images are the Signed RF output. Examples: Mickey Mouse versus a similar cartoon mouse, an origami crane versus a real crane, blurry versus sharp anime, and sad versus neutral portraits. Panel (h) is a grid of cat, ball and flamingo images that compares generations and their nearest training images with and without repulsion. Each panel has a caption that names the negative target π⁻. The eye goes first to the large image pairs.
caption: Signed Rectified Flow steers samples toward the positive target π+ while avoiding regions where the negative target π−dominates. Top row: 2D toy examples. (a) suppresses an undesired mode; (b) strengthens the desired target mode; and (c) avoids generating protected data. Bottom row: image-generation examples. (d) preserves cartoon attributes in π+ (round black ears, red shorts, yellow shoes) while avoiding the copyrighted character identity in π−; (e) preserves a paper-crane scene in π+ while avoiding a folded-paper appearance in π−; (f)–(g) suppress undesired visual attributes in π−; and (h) mitigates data leakage by repelling samples from the training set.
abstract: We introduce Signed Rectified Flow (Signed RF), a generalization of Rectified Flow that targets the signed measure $Ï^{sign} = (1+Î±)Ï^+ - Î±Ï^-$, where $Î±>0$, $Ï^+$ is the distribution to promote, and $Ï^-$ is the distribution to suppress. Although direct sampling from a signed measure is not well-defined, Signed RF induces a valid generative process that concentrates probability in regions where the signed measure is positive while provably excluding regions dominated by its negative component. It therefore provides a principled framework for incorporating negative information and exclusion constraints into generative modeling. We analyze the signed continuity equation underlying Signed RF and use a charged-particle interpretation to explain how negative mass forms exclusion barriers. This theory further motivates practical adaptive guidance algorithms. Across several applications, Signed RF improves the fidelity-diversity trade-off on ImageNet, reduces nearest-neighbor similarity in anti-memorization experiments, and reduces nudity induced by adversarial prompts in Stable Diffusion 3.5 while preserving CLIP and aesthetic scores.
